title: Making flying better for the environment
paragraphs: Flying has shrunk the world! It's now possible to travel around the globe quickly and easily. Jumping on a plane and jetting off on holiday or a business trip is the norm for many of us, and with the rise of budget airlines, the number of people taking to the skies is increasing. But while air travel is costing us less, the cost to the environment is going up.

Climate change is something we're all aware of now, and aviation companies know that some of the blame for this is being pointed at them. Last year commercial airlines were forecasted to use about 97bn gallons of jet fuel. But while we could think twice about taking a flight in the first place, particularly a short-haul trip that could be made by train, technology might be the answer to reducing emissions and minimising the environmental damage.

Recent developments have focussed on reducing the amount of fuel airliners burn. Making flying green and sustainable was the hot topic at the recent Dubai Air Show. There was talk of advances in engine technology, making them more efficient, and possibly using biofuel to power aircraft. Alejandro Rios Galvan, a bioenergy expert and professor at Khalifa University in Abu Dhabi, told the BBC that "these have the capacity to reduce the carbon footprint anywhere between 50-80% when you compare them to fossil (fuels)." And Phil Curnock, chief engineer of the civil future programme at Rolls-Royce, also suggested that electric hybrid engines could play a part for smaller aircraft, covering shorter distances. He says "it offers the possibility of a carbon-neutral flight for a limited range."

Being carbon neutral is the ultimate goal for the aviation industry, and one British airline, Easyjet, has recently said it would become the world's first major net zero carbon airline by offsetting carbon emissions.

Of course, aircraft manufacturers are constantly looking at ways to make their planes more fuel efficient. Boeing's Dreamliner, for example, is already in operation and uses 25 per cent less fuel per passenger compared with aircraft of a similar size. Other improvements include better aircraft aerodynamics, changes to ways aircraft taxi on runways, and the use of lighter materials.

But if we can't kick the flying habit, it seems these are the developments we need to make in order to ensure air travel is as green as possible. But aviation experts agree it's going to take time. We're left with short-term action such as taxing flights, regulation or protest - or being grounded and not flying at all.

vocabulary.entry: aviation /ˌeɪviˈeɪʃn/ n. 航空；航空业
vocabulary.example: The aviation industry has been badly hit by the pandemic.
vocabulary.translation: 航空业受到了疫情的严重打击。

vocabulary.entry: budget airline /ˈbʌdʒɪt ˈeəlaɪn/ 廉价航空公司
vocabulary.example: We booked our tickets with a budget airline to save money.
vocabulary.translation: 我们为了省钱，通过廉价航空公司预订了机票。

vocabulary.entry: take to the skies /teɪk tu ðə skaɪz/ 起飞；开始飞行（此处指选择空中出行）
vocabulary.example: Thousands of passengers take to the skies during the holiday season.
vocabulary.translation: 假期期间，成千上万的乘客选择坐飞机出行。

vocabulary.entry: emission /iˈmɪʃn/ n. 排放；排放物
vocabulary.example: The government has introduced new laws to reduce carbon emissions.
vocabulary.translation: 政府出台了新法律以减少碳排放。

vocabulary.entry: minimise /ˈmɪnɪmaɪz/ v. 使减到最少；最小化
vocabulary.example: We need to minimise the risk of accidents in the workplace.
vocabulary.translation: 我们需要将工作场所的事故风险降到最低。

vocabulary.entry: biofuel /ˈbaɪəʊfjuːəl/ n. 生物燃料
vocabulary.example: The company is investing in research into biofuel for cars.
vocabulary.translation: 该公司正在投资研发汽车用生物燃料。

vocabulary.entry: carbon footprint /ˈkɑːbən ˈfʊtprɪnt/ 碳足迹（指个人或组织的碳排放总量）
vocabulary.example: Eating less meat is one way to reduce your carbon footprint.
vocabulary.translation: 少吃肉类是减少碳足迹的一种方式。

vocabulary.entry: fossil fuel /ˈfɒsl fjuːəl/ 化石燃料（如煤、石油、天然气）
vocabulary.example: The world needs to move away from fossil fuels and towards renewable energy.
vocabulary.translation: 世界需要摆脱化石燃料，转向可再生能源。

vocabulary.entry: hybrid engine /ˈhaɪbrɪd ˈendʒɪn/ 混合动力发动机
vocabulary.example: This car is powered by a hybrid engine that uses both petrol and electricity.
vocabulary.translation: 这辆车搭载了汽油和电力两用的混合动力发动机。

vocabulary.entry: carbon-neutral /ˈkɑːbən njuːtrəl/ adj. 碳中和的（指碳排放与抵消量相等）
vocabulary.example: The company aims to become carbon-neutral by 2030.
vocabulary.translation: 该公司计划到2030年实现碳中和。

vocabulary.entry: net zero carbon /net ˈzɪərəʊ ˈkɑːbən/ 净零碳（指碳排放总量为零）
vocabulary.example: Many countries have pledged to achieve net zero carbon emissions by 2050.
vocabulary.translation: 许多国家承诺到2050年实现净零碳排放。

vocabulary.entry: offset /ˈɒfset/ v. 抵消；弥补（此处指抵消碳排放）
vocabulary.example: The company offsets its carbon emissions by planting trees.
vocabulary.translation: 该公司通过植树来抵消其碳排放。

vocabulary.entry: fuel-efficient /ˈfjuːəl ɪˈfɪʃnt/ adj. 省油的；节能的
vocabulary.example: This new model is more fuel-efficient than the older version.
vocabulary.translation: 这款新型号比旧款更省油。

vocabulary.entry: aerodynamics /ˌeərədaɪˈnæmɪks/ n. 空气动力学
vocabulary.example: The design of the car has been improved for better aerodynamics.
vocabulary.translation: 这款车的设计经过了优化，以提升空气动力学性能。

vocabulary.entry: taxi /ˈtæksi/ v. （飞机）在跑道滑行
vocabulary.example: The plane taxied down the runway before taking off.
vocabulary.translation: 飞机在跑道上滑行后起飞。

vocabulary.entry: lighter materials /ˈlaɪtə(r) məˈtɪəriəlz/ 更轻便的材料

vocabulary.translation: 使用更轻便的材料有助于减轻飞机重量，节省燃油。

vocabulary.entry: kick the habit /kɪk ðə ˈhæbɪt/ 戒除习惯

vocabulary.translation: 20年后，他终于戒掉了抽烟的习惯。

vocabulary.translation: 航空专家警告说，空域过度拥挤存在风险。

vocabulary.example: Some countries are considering taxing flights to reduce carbon emissions.
vocabulary.translation: 一些国家正考虑对航班征税，以减少碳排放。

vocabulary.entry: regulation /ˌreɡjuˈleɪʃn/ n. 法规；规章
vocabulary.example: The government has introduced new regulations for the aviation industry.
vocabulary.translation: 政府为航空业出台了新的法规。

vocabulary.entry: grounded /ɡraʊndɪd/ adj. 停飞的；不能飞行的
vocabulary.example: All flights were grounded due to bad weather.
vocabulary.translation: 由于天气恶劣，所有航班都被停飞。

vocabulary.entry: short-haul trip /ˌʃɔːt hɔːl trɪp/ 短途旅行
vocabulary.example: For a short-haul trip, taking the train is often cheaper and more environmentally friendly.
vocabulary.translation: 对于短途旅行，坐火车通常更便宜，也更环保。

title: Talking to strangers
paragraphs: ‘It’s good to talk’, so some people say. When I commute into London, there are certainly plenty of people conversing on their mobile phones – sometimes too loudly – discussing and sharing personal details with a friend. For me, it’s strange that they talk as though the person is sitting next to them, when they don’t even acknowledge the person who is actually sitting beside them.

Many of us spend part of each day surrounded by strangers, whether on our daily commute, or sitting in a park or a cafe. But most of them remain just that – strangers. However, new evidence has shown that plucking up the courage to strike up a conversation might be good for our health.

Nicholas Epley from the University of Chicago and Juliana Schroeder from the University of California are behavioural scientists. They looked at this silent relationship and whether solitude is a more positive experience than interacting with strangers, or if people misunderstand the consequences of distant social connections. They found that many people feel uncomfortable and intimidated talking to others and their research suggested that when we make an initial conversation “we consistently underestimate how much a new person likes us.” It seems we carry a negative voice in our head telling us all the things that could go wrong and why someone wouldn’t want to converse with us.

Their research involved an experiment with a group of Chicago commuters and found that “every participant in our experiment who actually tried to talk to a stranger found the person sitting next to them was happy to chat.” From this and other research, the conclusion is that connecting with strangers is surprisingly pleasant and it has a positive impact on our wellbeing. Gillian Sandstrom, a social psychologist from Essex University in the UK, told the BBC that “people are in a better mood after they reach out and have a conversation, however minimal.” It’s true that talking can make you feel happier and happiness can lead to better mental health.

However, if you’re an introvert, the thought of speaking to someone new might make you anxious. But the American research found “both extroverts and introverts are happier when they are asked to behave in an extroverted manner.” So maybe, if you’re a loner, it’s time to come out of your shell and make some small talk with a stranger – it could be the beginning of a new friendship.

vocabulary.entry: commute /kəˈmjuːt/ v. 通勤
vocabulary.example: She commutes from Oxford to London every day.
vocabulary.translation: 她每天从牛津通勤去伦敦上班。

vocabulary.entry: converse /kənˈvɜːs/ v. 交谈；谈话
vocabulary.example: We conversed for hours on a wide range of topics.
vocabulary.translation: 我们聊了好几个小时，话题涉猎甚广。

vocabulary.entry: personal detail /ˈpɜːsənl dɪˈteɪl/ n. 个人琐事
vocabulary.example: He refused to reveal any personal details about his family.
vocabulary.translation: 他拒绝透露任何关于自己家庭的个人琐事。

vocabulary.entry: acknowledge /əkˈnɒlɪdʒ/ v. 理睬；对……打招呼
vocabulary.example: He acknowledged her with a brief nod.
vocabulary.translation: 他对她略一点头，算是打了招呼。

vocabulary.entry: pluck up the courage /plʌk ʌp ðə ˈkʌrɪdʒ/ 鼓起勇气
vocabulary.example: She plucked up the courage to ask for a pay rise.
vocabulary.translation: 她鼓起勇气要求加薪。

vocabulary.entry: strike up a conversation /straɪk ʌp ə ˌkɒnvəˈseɪʃn/ 开启对话；主动搭话
vocabulary.example: He struck up a conversation with the man sitting next to him on the train.
vocabulary.translation: 他在火车上主动和坐在身边的男士攀谈起来。

vocabulary.entry: behavioural scientist /bɪˈheɪvjərəl ˈsaɪəntɪst/ n. 行为科学家
vocabulary.example: The behavioural scientist is conducting research on human social interactions.
vocabulary.translation: 这位行为科学家正在开展关于人类社交互动的研究。

vocabulary.entry: solitude /ˈsɒlɪtjuːd/ n. 独处；独居
vocabulary.example: She enjoys the solitude of her own flat.
vocabulary.translation: 她很享受在自己公寓里的独处时光。

vocabulary.entry: interact /ˌɪntərˈækt/ v. 互动；交流
vocabulary.example: The teacher interacts well with her students.
vocabulary.translation: 这位老师和学生们互动得很融洽。

vocabulary.entry: distant social connection /ˈdɪstənt ˈsəʊʃl kəˈnekʃn/ n. 疏远的社交关系
vocabulary.example: Distant social connection may not bring people a sense of belonging.
vocabulary.translation: 疏远的社交关系或许无法给人带来归属感。

vocabulary.entry: consequence /ˈkɒnsɪkwəns/ n. 影响；后果
vocabulary.example: The environmental consequences of this policy could be disastrous.
vocabulary.translation: 这项政策可能会带来灾难性的环境影响。

vocabulary.entry: intimidate /ɪnˈtɪmɪdeɪt/ v. 使胆怯；使害怕
vocabulary.example: She was intimidated by the number of people watching her.
vocabulary.translation: 看着她的人很多，这让她很胆怯。

vocabulary.entry: initial /ɪˈnɪʃl/ adj. 初步的；开始的
vocabulary.example: The initial reaction to the plan was positive.
vocabulary.translation: 大家对这个计划的初步反应是积极的。

vocabulary.entry: consistently /kənˈsɪstəntli/ adv. 一贯地；始终如一地
vocabulary.example: The company has consistently improved its services over the years.
vocabulary.translation: 这家公司多年来一直在持续改进服务。

vocabulary.entry: underestimate /ˌʌndərˈestɪmeɪt/ v. 低估
vocabulary.example: Never underestimate the power of human curiosity.
vocabulary.translation: 永远不要低估人类好奇心的力量。

vocabulary.entry: participant /pɑːˈtɪsɪpənt/ n. 参与者
vocabulary.example: All participants will receive a certificate of completion.
vocabulary.translation: 所有参与者都会得到一份结业证书。

vocabulary.entry: positive impact /ˈpɒzətɪv ˈɪmpækt/ n. 积极影响
vocabulary.example: Regular exercise has a positive impact on mental health.
vocabulary.translation: 规律运动对心理健康有积极影响。

vocabulary.entry: wellbeing /ˈwelbiːɪŋ/ n. 身心健康；幸福
vocabulary.example: A balanced diet is essential for good health and wellbeing.
vocabulary.translation: 均衡饮食对良好的健康和身心状态至关重要。

vocabulary.entry: reach out /riːtʃ aʊt/ 主动联系；主动搭话
vocabulary.example: It's important to reach out to friends when you're feeling lonely.
vocabulary.translation: 感到孤独时，主动联系朋友很重要。

vocabulary.entry: minimal /ˈmɪnɪməl/ adj. 极小的；极少的
vocabulary.example: The damage to the building was minimal.
vocabulary.translation: 这栋建筑的损坏程度很小。

vocabulary.entry: introvert /ˈɪntrəvɜːt/ n. 内向的人
vocabulary.example: As an introvert, he prefers quiet activities to noisy parties.
vocabulary.translation: 作为一个内向的人，比起喧闹的派对，他更喜欢安静的活动。

vocabulary.entry: extrovert /ˈekstrəvɜːt/ n. 外向的人
vocabulary.example: Her sister is a cheerful extrovert who makes friends easily.
vocabulary.translation: 她的姐姐是个开朗的外向者，很容易交到朋友。

vocabulary.entry: extroverted manner /ˈekstrəvɜːtɪd ˈmænə/ n. 外向的行事方式
vocabulary.example: Adopting an extroverted manner helped her make more friends.
vocabulary.translation: 采取外向的行事方式帮她交到了更多朋友。

vocabulary.entry: loner /ˈləʊnə/ n. 喜欢独处的人；独来独往者
vocabulary.example: He's always been a bit of a loner, preferring his own company.
vocabulary.translation: 他向来有点独来独往，更喜欢一个人待着。

vocabulary.example: The trip helped her come out of her shell and meet new people.
vocabulary.translation: 这次旅行让她敞开心扉，结识了不少新朋友。

sentences.chinese: 他们研究了这种“沉默的关系”，探究独处是否比与陌生人互动更积极，以及人们是否误解了疏远的社交关系所带来的影响。

sentences.english: They found that many people feel uncomfortable and intimidated talking to others and their research suggested that when we make an initial conversation “we consistently underestimate how much a new person likes us.”
sentences.chinese: 他们发现，很多人在与他人交谈时会感到不适和胆怯，而他们的研究表明，当我们主动开启第一次对话时，“我们总是低估陌生人对我们的好感度”。

sentences.english: It seems we carry a negative voice in our head telling us all the things that could go wrong and why someone wouldn’t want to converse with us.
sentences.chinese: 似乎我们脑海里总有一个负面的声音，告诉我们所有可能出错的事情，以及别人为什么不想和我们交谈。

sentences.english: Their research involved an experiment with a group of Chicago commuters and found that “every participant in our experiment who actually tried to talk to a stranger found the person sitting next to them was happy to chat.”
sentences.chinese: 他们的研究包括一项针对芝加哥通勤者的实验，结果是“实验中每一个真正尝试与陌生人交谈的参与者，都发现坐在身边的人很乐意聊天”。

sentences.english: From this and other research, the conclusion is that connecting with strangers is surprisingly pleasant and it has a positive impact on our wellbeing.
sentences.chinese: 从这项研究和其他研究中得出的结论是，与陌生人交流令人意外地愉快，并且对我们的身心健康有积极影响。

sentences.english: Gillian Sandstrom, a social psychologist from Essex University in the UK, told the BBC that “people are in a better mood after they reach out and have a conversation, however minimal.”
sentences.chinese: 英国埃塞克斯大学的社会心理学家吉莉安·桑德斯特伦向英国广播公司表示：“当人们主动进行交谈时，无论对话多么简短，他们的心情都会变得更好。”

sentences.english: It’s true that talking can make you feel happier and happiness can lead to better mental health.
sentences.chinese: 的确，交谈能让你感到更快乐，而快乐有助于提升心理健康水平。

sentences.english: However, if you’re an introvert, the thought of speaking to someone new might make you anxious.
sentences.chinese: 但如果你是一个内向的人，一想到要和陌生人说话，可能就会感到焦虑。

sentences.english: But the American research found “both extroverts and introverts are happier when they are asked to behave in an extroverted manner.”
sentences.chinese: 不过这项美国研究发现，“无论是外向者还是内向者，当他们尝试以更外向的方式行事时，都会感到更快乐”。

sentences.english: So maybe, if you’re a loner, it’s time to come out of your shell and make some small talk with a stranger – it could be the beginning of a new friendship.
sentences.chinese: 所以，如果你是一个喜欢独处的人，或许是时候敞开心扉，和陌生人聊几句闲话了——这或许会成为一段新友谊的开端。

title: Natural therapy
titleChinese: 治疗心理疾病的天然疗法
paragraphs: The great outdoors: it’s the place to head for when you’re in need of peace and quiet, open spaces, beautiful scenery and exercise. Whether a huge mountain range or a local country park, these natural areas are a perfect tonic for our stressed-out lives, and their therapeutic effect is being used more and more to treat mental health.

As an example, in the foothills of the Snowdonia National Park in the UK, specialist therapy sessions are held to help people who suffer from depression, anxiety and stress. Outdoor art-related activities are held for patients, but the setting alone has been credited with improving the mood of patients. Art psychotherapist Pamela Stanley told the BBC that there was a "growing body of evidence" to support eco-therapy.

It’s true that for most of us connecting with the natural world definitely lifts our spirits. But the mental health charity Mind says eco-therapy has been recognised as a formal type of treatment that can sometimes be prescribed to someone by a doctor. It doesn’t involve taking medication, but instead it just develops a person’s relationship with nature. This natural remedy can take on many forms, but can include doing yoga in a forest, gardening or even hugging a tree.

Evidence has shown there are many benefits of this ‘green’ therapy, including improving social contact, social and work skills and coping abilities. It’s what Dr Rachel Bragg from the University of Essex calls ‘psychological restoration’. She told the BBC’s All in the Mind programme that nature-based therapies should be part of a "toolkit" of care for patients.

One reason why getting back to nature is, well, natural, is something called biophilia, a sort of understanding or empathy with the natural world. According to environmental psychologist Birgitta Gatersleben, “the idea that nature reminds us of life, and if we (are) exposed to the natural elements, then our sort of negative feelings get almost immediately replaced with positive emotions.”

title: Why take a gap year
paragraphs: When you’ve finished your studies at school and college, do you feel like a well-earned rest? If you’re about to embark on a course at university, you’ll want to recharge your batteries, let your hair down and have some fun. But how long should you do that for? Now the idea of taking a year off before you move into further education seems to be the thing to do.

A year off – also called a gap year – is not a new concept, but there’s now a focus on making the most of this break from academic life. Long gone are the days of just hanging out on a beach or backpacking round the world. While that is still an option, a gap year is now more about gaining skills that will help you in later life. The BBC’s Smart Consumer podcast spoke to a student called Meg, who said “I just always had in the back of my mind I'd spend a year doing something productive and something that would just be good fun.”

Doing something productive is exactly what students are being encouraged to do because doing more purposeful things like work experience or charity work helps them acquire skills to use when competing for a place at university. It looks good on their CV and ultimately makes them more employable. Chris Rea is a Higher Education Services Manager from organisation, Prospects. He told the BBC that he thinks “the experience of the gap year has become actually much more practical, partly to do with university participation increasing, but also because of the demands on developing skills, specifically employability skills.”

While the benefits of taking a gap year are clear to see, some students worry they can’t afford it. Another student, Tom, told the BBC that to him, a gap year was an ‘alien concept’. He said “it would have been far too expensive and it's not something that I would have been able to rely on my parents or family members for.” But some experts say that it needn’t burn a hole in your pocket; you don’t need to travel far and you can even earn money by doing paid work.

For those who do have the funds, a combination of working, volunteering and travelling is undoubtedly an amazing opportunity. It increases confidence and independence, gives you a chance to learn new crafts, and gives you time to contemplate whether university is right for you.

sentences.chinese: 休学一年——也被称为间隔年——并不是什么新概念，但现在人们更注重充分利用这段脱离学术生活的假期。

sentences.english: Long gone are the days of just hanging out on a beach or backpacking round the world.
sentences.chinese: 仅仅是在海滩休闲或环球背包旅行的日子早已过去。

sentences.english: While that is still an option, a gap year is now more about gaining skills that will help you in later life.
sentences.chinese: 虽然这些仍是可选方案，但如今的间隔年更侧重于获取对未来生活有益的技能。

sentences.english: The BBC’s Smart Consumer podcast spoke to a student called Meg, who said “I just always had in the back of my mind I'd spend a year doing something productive and something that would just be good fun.”
sentences.chinese: 英国广播公司《精明消费者》播客采访了一位名叫梅格的学生，她说：“我心底深处一直在想，要花一年时间做些有意义且有趣的事。”
underlinedTerms: in the back of my mind

sentences.english: Doing something productive is exactly what students are being encouraged to do because doing more purposeful things like work experience or charity work helps them acquire skills to use when competing for a place at university.
sentences.chinese: 鼓励学生们做些有意义的事，因为参与工作实习、慈善活动等更具目的性的项目，能帮助他们获得申请大学时所需的技能。

sentences.english: It looks good on their CV and ultimately makes them more employable.
sentences.chinese: 这会让他们的个人简历更具吸引力，最终提升就业竞争力。

sentences.english: Chris Rea is a Higher Education Services Manager from organisation, Prospects. He told the BBC that he thinks “the experience of the gap year has become actually much more practical, partly to do with university participation increasing, but also because of the demands on developing skills, specifically employability skills.”
sentences.chinese: 英国职业规划机构Prospects的高等教育服务经理克里斯·雷向英国广播公司表示：“间隔年的经历实际上变得更加实用，一方面是因为上大学的人数增多，另一方面是因为社会对技能培养的需求，尤其是就业技能。”

sentences.english: While the benefits of taking a gap year are clear to see, some students worry they can’t afford it.
sentences.chinese: 尽管间隔年的好处显而易见，但有些学生担心自己负担不起。

sentences.english: Another student, Tom, told the BBC that to him, a gap year was an ‘alien concept’.
sentences.chinese: 另一位学生汤姆告诉英国广播公司，对他来说，间隔年是一个“陌生的概念”。

sentences.english: He said “it would have been far too expensive and it's not something that I would have been able to rely on my parents or family members for.”
sentences.chinese: 他说：“这实在太贵了，我也不能依赖父母或家人来承担这笔费用。”

sentences.english: But some experts say that it needn’t burn a hole in your pocket; you don’t need to travel far and you can even earn money by doing paid work.
sentences.chinese: 但一些专家表示，间隔年并不需要花费巨资；你不必远行，甚至可以通过有偿工作赚取收入。
underlinedTerms: burn a hole in your pocket

sentences.english: For those who do have the funds, a combination of working, volunteering and travelling is undoubtedly an amazing opportunity.
sentences.chinese: 对于那些有经济能力的人来说，将工作、志愿服务和旅行结合起来的间隔年无疑是一次绝佳的机会。

sentences.english: It increases confidence and independence, gives you a chance to learn new crafts, and gives you time to contemplate whether university is right for you.
sentences.chinese: 它能增强你的自信心和独立性，让你有机会学习新技能，并有时间思考大学是否真的适合自己。

title: Smartphone vs the classroom
titleChinese: 智能手机 vs 传统课堂
paragraphs: We know it’s good to learn another language. It opens doors, makes you more employable, helps you make new friends, and it’s fun too. But to improve our linguistic skills, many of us have to endure hours of school lessons or evening classes, with our heads buried in textbooks. It’s no wonder then that technology appears to be providing a better and more accessible way of learning.

There is certainly a huge demand for language learning, and having a smartphone means you can have a virtual teacher with you wherever you go. Many app developers are keen to cash in on the demand, and there are numerous learning apps available – including our own, free, BBC Learning English app! One of many popular apps, Duolingo, offers 91 courses in 30 languages and has more than 300 million users.

Some educational apps offer languages not popular enough to be taught at evening classes, or at most universities. And others offer ‘invented’ language courses in Esperanto, Elvish and Star Trek's Klingon – lessons you might not find in a traditional classroom. Whatever you want to learn, apps allow you to go at your own pace and fit learning around other commitments. But they’re not perfect – you might not get your head round the grammar and will lack the peer support you could get in a classroom environment.

So, does technology spell the end of traditional classrooms and teachers? Guy Baron, head of modern languages at Aberystwyth University, thinks not. He told the BBC that apps should be used alongside classroom methods, not to the exclusion of traditional teaching. And he adds: "The apps are very conversational... they're not designed for degrees, but they could be additional resources."

Certainly technology is going to help in and outside the classroom. But attending a real lesson, facing a real teacher, probably forces you to be more committed. Motivation can be a problem when using an app. But if you have a genuine and practical reason to learn another language, you will no doubt stick with it.

vocabulary.entry: peer support /pɪə(r) səˈpɔːt/ 同伴支持；同侪互助

vocabulary.translation: 他一心扑在工作上，排除了所有其他兴趣爱好。

vocabulary.translation: 这款应用提供口语对话练习，帮助用户更自然地表达。

title: Ancestry travel
paragraphs: Everyone loves a holiday! A little time off for some much-needed R & R can be exactly the thing to rejuvenate and refresh. That said, if you're struggling to think of your next destination then look no further. Don't waste time debating, let your blood decide.

Everybody has a lineage. Recently, finding out more about our family origins has become popular. By the start of 2019, 26 million people had taken an ancestry DNA test at home, according to a report by MIT Technology Review. They believe by 2021 this number will have risen to 100 million.

This trend has been noticed by opportunistic travel operators. Some are looking to provide a service that both allows people to trace their heritage - by literally going back to their roots - and travel to the destinations where their ancestors originated from.

Airbnb, an online lodging marketplace, recently partnered with 23andMe, a DNA testing and analysis company, to offer recommendations that encourage travellers to walk in the footsteps of their forefathers. And they aren't the only ones.

The Shelbourne hotel in Dublin has its own 'genealogy butler'. Hellen Kelly offers consultations to help guests trace their Irish line of descent using official records. This allows them to 'fill in the blanks of their Irish ancestry', she told Good Morning America.

The Conte Club, a luxury travel company, offers custom itineraries based on DNA tests. 'These experiences are about delving deeper into who we really are,' says Conte Club CEO Rebecca Fielding in an article in the Condé Nast Traveller. 'It might be the most meaningful trip we can take.'
So next time you think of going on vacation, why not take a DNA test first? Once you know how far your family has come, take the time to holiday back.

vocabulary.entry: R & R (Rest and Relaxation) /ˌɑː(r) ənd ˈɑː(r)/ 休息放松（常用缩写）
vocabulary.example: After the busy project, we all needed some R & R at the beach.
vocabulary.translation: 繁忙的项目结束后，我们都需要去海滩休息放松一下。

vocabulary.entry: rejuvenate /rɪˈdʒuːvəneɪt/ v. 恢复活力；使焕发青春
vocabulary.example: A weekend in the countryside can rejuvenate even the most tired city dwellers.
vocabulary.translation: 在乡下度过一个周末，即便是最疲惫的城市居民也能恢复活力。

vocabulary.entry: lineage /ˈlɪniɪdʒ/ n. 家族谱系；血统
vocabulary.example: She can trace her lineage back to the 17th-century nobility.
vocabulary.translation: 她能将自己的家族谱系追溯到17世纪的贵族。

vocabulary.entry: family origins /ˈfæməli ˈɒrɪdʒɪnz/ 家族起源；祖籍
vocabulary.example: He traveled to India to learn more about his family origins.
vocabulary.translation: 他前往印度，想要更多地了解自己的家族起源。

vocabulary.entry: ancestry DNA test /ˈænsestri ˌdiː en ˈeɪ test/ 祖先DNA检测
vocabulary.example: Many people take an ancestry DNA test to discover their ethnic background.
vocabulary.translation: 很多人通过祖先DNA检测来了解自己的种族背景。

vocabulary.entry: opportunistic /ˌɒpəˈtjuːnɪstɪk/ adj.  opportunistic（善于抓住机会的；投机的）
vocabulary.example: The company made an opportunistic move to enter the growing market.
vocabulary.translation: 该公司抓住机会，进入了这个不断增长的市场。

vocabulary.entry: trace their heritage /treɪs ðeə(r) ˈherɪtɪdʒ/ 追溯家族传承；探寻文化遗产
vocabulary.example: She spent years researching to trace her heritage in Scotland.
vocabulary.translation: 她花了数年时间研究，追溯自己在苏格兰的家族传承。

vocabulary.entry: go back to their roots /ɡəʊ bæk tu ðeə(r) ruːts/ 回到根源；寻根
vocabulary.example: After living abroad for 20 years, he decided to go back to his roots in China.
vocabulary.translation: 在国外生活了20年后，他决定回到中国寻根。

vocabulary.entry: originate from /əˈrɪdʒɪneɪt frəm/ 起源于；来自
vocabulary.example: The tradition is believed to originate from ancient Rome.
vocabulary.translation: 这个传统被认为起源于古罗马。

vocabulary.entry: partner with /ˈpɑːtnə(r) wɪð/ 与……合作
vocabulary.example: The museum partnered with a local school to offer educational programs.
vocabulary.translation: 博物馆与当地一所学校合作，推出教育项目。

vocabulary.entry: walk in the footsteps of /wɔːk ɪn ðə ˈfʊtsteps ɒv/ 追随……的脚步；效仿
vocabulary.example: She dreamed of walking in the footsteps of her grandmother, who was a famous writer.
vocabulary.translation: 她梦想追随祖母的脚步，祖母是一位著名作家。

vocabulary.entry: forefathers /ˈfɔːfɑːðəz/ n. 祖先；前辈
vocabulary.example: Our forefathers built this village with their own hands.
vocabulary.translation: 我们的祖先用自己的双手建造了这个村庄。

vocabulary.entry: genealogy butler /ˌdʒiːniˈælədʒi ˈbʌtlə(r)/ 谱系管家（专门协助追溯家族谱系的服务人员）
vocabulary.example: The luxury hotel’s genealogy butler helped guests research their family trees.
vocabulary.translation: 这家豪华酒店的谱系管家帮助客人研究家族谱系。

vocabulary.entry: consultation /ˌkɒnsəlˈteɪʃn/ n. 咨询；磋商

vocabulary.translation: 她预约了一位谱系专家进行咨询，以追溯自己的祖先。

vocabulary.entry: line of descent /laɪn ɒv dɪˈsent/ 血统；世系
vocabulary.example: The king’s line of descent can be traced back over 1000 years.
vocabulary.translation: 这位国王的血统可以追溯到1000多年前。

vocabulary.entry: fill in the blanks /fɪl ɪn ðə blæŋks/ 填补空白；补齐缺失信息
vocabulary.example: The old letters helped fill in the blanks about his grandfather’s life.
vocabulary.translation: 这些旧信件帮助补齐了关于他祖父生平的缺失信息。

vocabulary.entry: custom itinerary /ˈkʌstəm aɪˈtɪnərəri/ 定制旅行路线
vocabulary.example: The travel agency created a custom itinerary for their honeymoon trip.
vocabulary.translation: 旅行社为他们的蜜月旅行定制了专属路线。

vocabulary.entry: delve deeper into /delv ˈdiːpə(r) ˈɪntuː/ 深入探索；深入研究
vocabulary.example: The documentary delves deeper into the history of the ancient civilization.
vocabulary.translation: 这部纪录片深入探索了这个古代文明的历史。

vocabulary.entry: meaningful /ˈmiːnɪŋfl/ adj. 有意义的；意味深长的
vocabulary.example: Volunteering in the community was a meaningful experience for her.
vocabulary.translation: 在社区做志愿服务对她来说是一次有意义的经历。

vocabulary.entry: vacation /vəˈkeɪʃn/ n. 假期；休假（美式英语常用）

title: Why do we yawn
paragraphs: Yawning is something we all do – maybe because we’re bored carrying out tedious tasks or because we’re tired. Sometimes, just seeing other people yawn can set you off. But is this biological function really contagious, and why do we do it in the first place?

Many of us think we open our mouths when we yawn to take in more oxygen, but in fact it appears there is no clear biological reason. According to BBC Bitesize, new research suggests it might be because yawning cools the brain down and prevents it from overheating, much like the fan in your laptop. This might be why we’re more likely to feel drowsy and yawn in warm temperatures.

What is clear is that we yawn more when we’re exhausted and ready for a nap, and we can’t control when we do it – once we start, there’s no stopping us! But it’s also true that yawning is a very contagious behaviour. John Drury, a researcher from Sussex University, told the BBC that “it’s meant to be automatic; it’s something that you can’t stop. Dogs yawn when their owners yawn, animals yawn to each other. It happens whether you want to or not.”

His research into this cognitive behaviour found that there is a connection with our social group and how close we are to the people in it. If we identify with the person who exhibits the behaviour, we are likely to copy it too.

Other research by the University of Nottingham in 2017 found similar results. They asked volunteers to watch other people yawn. They found their ability to resist yawning when others around them yawned was limited. And the urge to yawn was increased when people were told they couldn’t. They also found, when using electrical stimulation, that they were able to increase people’s desire to yawn. These findings, they say, could be useful because it could help treat other conditions like Tourette’s, which involve the same area of the brain.
What is certain is that a yawn can creep up on us at any time even when we think we’re not tired – but, I hope, not when you’re reading this article!

title: Should we talk about our salaries
titleChinese: 同事之间工资应该公开吗？
paragraphs: It's a touchy subject. Talking socially about money can make people feel uncomfortable. But at work, have a conversation about how much people earn, and things can not only get awkward, but, in some cases, it can get you sacked.

According to a survey by the Trades Union Congress, 1 in 5 workers "have been told they can’t talk about their pay at work". This, concludes the TUC, indicates how common pay secrecy or 'gagging' clauses are in employment contracts. 'Pay secrecy clauses are a get out of jail free card for bad bosses,' said TUC general secretary Frances O'Grady. 'They stop workers from challenging unfair pay, allow top executives to hoard profits and encourage discrimination. More openness about wages is essential to building fairer workplaces.'

So, should we talk about how much we earn? It's not so simple. Even without the contractual obligations, people may still be reluctant. "I personally have found it's better not looking and not knowing," Tracy Jordan, an HR professional, told the BBC. "Even if you feel you are paid a fair wage, there will always be someone that you perceive is doing a lesser job and is earning more. Rather than feeling perpetually dissatisfied, I think ignorance can be bliss."

Money is tied up with complex emotions, Brianna McGurran, a money expert at the personal finance blog NerdWallet, told the New York Times. It involves emotions like shame, success and fear of failure. It also influences how people view you. People's money is tied to their self-worth. As a result, culturally, it can be bit of a taboo.

But all that may change. First of all, pay secrecy clauses are unenforceable in the UK due to the UK Equality Act 2010. An employee must always be able to find out if they are being discriminated against in terms of pay. In addition, The European Union is considering new legislation on pay transparency in order to reduce gender pay, earnings and pension gaps. So, for better or worse it may be something we all have to get used to. Over time, talking about our salaries may become just another matter for small talk.

title: Working from home
paragraphs: If you go to work, you’re probably familiar with the routine of travelling to the office, hunting for an available desk, completing your tasks and then enduring your commute home. In many ways, it seems like an outdated working practice. And maybe that’s why more and more of us are now choosing to work from home.

There are, of course, many reasons for remote working, as it is also called. The demands of modern life and a desire for a better work-life balance has driven the trend, along with improved technology, which makes doing most tasks at home a doddle.

In the UK, figures from the Office for National Statistics show more than one and a half million people work from home for their main job. But, although logging on from the comfort of your sofa may appeal, especially if it’s part of a flexible working approach, some people are forced to work from home and find it hard going. Marketing consultant Mark Black told the BBC he struggled to switch off from work when he was based solely at home. He says: "I hated home working. You get up in the morning and stare at the same four walls, do your work, and try and clock off, but you can't." It’s true that being at home means you can’t physically leave your office behind, and as Emma Mamo from mental health charity Mind says: "Home workers don't always have the same opportunities to connect with people as their office-based colleagues.”

But remote working doesn’t always mean being at home. Cafes and workplace spaces offer a chance for workers, particularly self-employed people, to come together and interact with each other. There are also employees who have no choice but to work remotely because their companies have decided to do away with offices altogether to have a more agile workforce - it's certainly very cost effective and attractive for start-ups. But for those employed by businesses with a physical base, working at home provides a convenient alternative to the 9 to 5. And without the distraction of their colleagues, it can be the most productive place to work!

title: When should I have a sick day
paragraphs: Have you ever woken up with a sore throat and blocked nose and wondered if you should take the day off work? Some of us just soldier on, hoping the office environment and banter with work colleagues will perk us up. Others will make a hot drink, return to bed and have a ‘duvet day’. But what is the right approach to take?

People’s attitude to illness and when to take time off work varies. Reasons for having a sick day range from a light sniffle to feeling at death’s door. And when you have no genuine excuse but just can’t face going into work, it might be time to take a sickie. A survey of British workers by YouGov found 15% of workers who admitted making up an illness to get a day off used a migraine as their excuse. But what about a common cold – is having one a genuine enough reason for missing work?

This is something Ian Shoesmith explored for the BBC. He looked into “the murky moral maze” that brought together employment law, ethics and public health. He spoke to Rachel Suff, senior policy adviser at the Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development, who said "If you are really not well and your symptoms mean you are not going to be productive, it's better to go off sick. You're also not spreading your germs around the workplace." But Ian also found that catching a cold from someone could help build up your immune system and be good for long-term health. However it can depend on what type of cold it is.

Of course, deciding whether to take time off to recuperate from a cold may depend on where you work. Hayley Johnson, an employment lawyer at Slater and Gordon, told the BBC that sometimes members of staff feel obliged to work when they are sick "because they fear the mountain of work will just keep piling up" for when they return. But if an employee is feeling under the weather but well enough to work, a solution could be to work from home.
As a cure for a common cold is still a long way off, having this lurgy as an excuse for a day off work is not to be sneezed at!

vocabulary.translation: 经常洗手可以杀灭病菌。

vocabulary.entry: immune system /ɪˈmjuːn ˈsɪstəm/ 免疫系统
vocabulary.example: Eating a balanced diet helps boost your immune system.
vocabulary.translation: 均衡饮食有助于增强免疫系统。

vocabulary.entry: recuperate /rɪˈkjuːpəreɪt/ v. 康复；恢复健康
vocabulary.example: She went to the countryside to recuperate from her illness.
vocabulary.translation: 她去乡下养病，恢复健康。

vocabulary.entry: obliged /əˈblaɪdʒd/ adj. 有义务的；必须的
vocabulary.example: Employees are obliged to follow the company’s safety rules.
vocabulary.translation: 员工必须遵守公司的安全规定。

vocabulary.entry: pile up /paɪl ʌp/ 堆积；积压
vocabulary.example: Work tends to pile up at the end of the month.
vocabulary.translation: 月底的时候，工作往往会堆积如山。

vocabulary.entry: under the weather /ˈʌndə ðə ˈweðə/ 身体不适；有点小病
vocabulary.example: I’m feeling a bit under the weather so I won’t go out tonight.
vocabulary.translation: 我有点不舒服，今晚就不出去了。

vocabulary.entry: lurgy /ˈlɜːdʒi/ n. 小病；轻微传染病（口语）
vocabulary.example: A lot of people in the office have picked up a lurgy.
vocabulary.translation: 办公室里很多人都得了一种小病。

vocabulary.entry: not to be sneezed at /nɒt tu biː sniːzd æt/ 不容小觑；值得考虑
vocabulary.example: A bonus of £500 is not to be sneezed at.
vocabulary.translation: 500英镑的奖金可不是一笔小钱，不容小觑。

sentences.english: Have you ever woken up with a sore throat and blocked nose and wondered if you should take the day off work?
sentences.chinese: 你有没有过早上醒来嗓子疼、鼻子堵，还纠结要不要请假的经历？

sentences.english: Some of us just soldier on, hoping the office environment and banter with work colleagues will perk us up.
sentences.chinese: 有些人会选择硬撑着上班，盼着办公室的氛围和同事间的打趣能让自己精神起来。

sentences.english: Others will make a hot drink, return to bed and have a ‘duvet day’.
sentences.chinese: 还有些人会泡一杯热饮，回到床上，享受一个“被窝休息日”。

sentences.english: But what is the right approach to take?
sentences.chinese: 但到底哪种做法才是正确的呢？

sentences.english: People’s attitude to illness and when to take time off work varies.
sentences.chinese: 人们对于生病以及何时请假的态度各不相同。

sentences.english: Reasons for having a sick day range from a light sniffle to feeling at death’s door.
sentences.chinese: 请假的理由五花八门，从轻微的鼻塞流涕到感觉病入膏肓都有。

sentences.english: And when you have no genuine excuse but just can’t face going into work, it might be time to take a sickie.
sentences.chinese: 而当你没什么正当理由，只是实在不想上班的时候，或许就该“装病请假”了。

sentences.english: A survey of British workers by YouGov found 15% of workers who admitted making up an illness to get a day off used a migraine as their excuse.
sentences.chinese: 舆观调查公司针对英国职场人士的一项调查显示，在承认过编造病情请假的人中，有15%会用偏头痛当借口。

sentences.english: But what about a common cold – is having one a genuine enough reason for missing work?
sentences.chinese: 但普通感冒呢？它算得上是旷工的正当理由吗？

sentences.english: This is something Ian Shoesmith explored for the BBC.
sentences.chinese: 伊恩·休史密斯为英国广播公司探讨了这个问题。

sentences.english: He looked into “the murky moral maze” that brought together employment law, ethics and public health.
sentences.chinese: 他深入研究了这个交织着劳动法、道德规范和公共卫生的“晦暗的道德迷宫”。

sentences.english: He spoke to Rachel Suff, senior policy adviser at the Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development, who said "If you are really not well and your symptoms mean you are not going to be productive, it's better to go off sick.
sentences.chinese: 他采访了英国特许人事与发展协会的高级政策顾问蕾切尔·萨夫，对方表示：“如果你真的身体不适，而且症状已经影响到工作效率，那最好还是请假。

sentences.english: You're also not spreading your germs around the workplace."
sentences.chinese: 这样也不会把病菌传染给同事。”

sentences.english: But Ian also found that catching a cold from someone could help build up your immune system and be good for long-term health.
sentences.chinese: 但伊恩也发现，被他人传染感冒，其实有助于增强自身免疫系统，对长远健康有好处。

sentences.english: However it can depend on what type of cold it is.
sentences.chinese: 不过，这也取决于感冒的类型。

sentences.english: Of course, deciding whether to take time off to recuperate from a cold may depend on where you work.
sentences.chinese: 当然，感冒后要不要请假休养，可能还取决于你的工作环境。

sentences.english: Hayley Johnson, an employment lawyer at Slater and Gordon, told the BBC that sometimes members of staff feel obliged to work when they are sick "because they fear the mountain of work will just keep piling up" for when they return.
sentences.chinese: 斯莱特和戈登律师事务所的劳工律师海莉·约翰逊告诉英国广播公司，有时候员工生病也会硬撑着上班，“因为他们担心休假回来后，工作会堆积如山”。

sentences.english: But if an employee is feeling under the weather but well enough to work, a solution could be to work from home.
sentences.chinese: 但如果员工只是有些不舒服，身体状况还允许工作，那居家办公会是一个不错的选择。

sentences.english: As a cure for a common cold is still a long way off, having this lurgy as an excuse for a day off work is not to be sneezed at!
sentences.chinese: 既然彻底治愈普通感冒的方法还遥遥无期，那借着这场小感冒请一天假，也是值得考虑的一件事！

title: Unrealistic career aspirations
titleChinese: 英国年轻人不现实的职业理想
paragraphs: What did you want to be when you were growing up? A doctor, an engineer - or maybe a footballer or actor? We all had big plans for our futures and believed there was a dream job waiting for us – one that would pay well and give great job satisfaction. But how realistic was that?

Today, in the UK at least, young people are being warned that some of their career hopes and dreams don’t match the types of jobs available. Research by the charity Education and Employers suggests five times as many 17 and 18 year-olds in the UK want to work in art, culture, entertainment and sport than there are jobs.

The glamour and excitement of working in these employment sectors is obviously a draw. But those looking for these types of job will be ‘destined for disappointment’. That’s what the report, Disconnected: Career aspirations and jobs in the UK, says. Writing about this for the BBC, Katherine Sellgren points out that while young people are keen to work in art, entertainment, culture and sport, the economy is unlikely to need them all. In the meantime, there is a shortfall of young people wanting to work in careers such as catering and retail.

Previous research about the career aspirations of young people by the Office for National Statistics also found a ‘reality gap’ between their dreams and the sometimes disappointing truth by the time they reached their early to late-20s. Apart from those who aimed to go into teaching, fewer than one in 50 were in the jobs they had wanted – such as a doctor, vet, firefighter or actor. Most were working as sales assistants, carers or in sales and marketing.

While it’s good to have aspirations, the aims of young people need to be realistic. This latest report suggests that children need to be made more aware of a wider variety of occupations at a younger age. It also calls for improved careers advice in secondary schools. A spokeswoman for the Department for Work and Pensions told the BBC that “early careers advice can help young people set out on the right path to the job that channels their interests and unlocks their potential.”

vocabulary.entry: career aspiration /kəˈrɪə ˌæspəˈreɪʃn/ 职业理想；职业抱负
vocabulary.example: Young people's career aspirations are often shaped by their role models.
vocabulary.translation: 年轻人的职业理想往往会受到榜样人物的影响。

vocabulary.entry: glamour /ˈɡlæmə(r)/ n. 吸引力；魅力；光鲜亮丽
vocabulary.example: The glamour of city life is a magnet for many young people from rural areas.
vocabulary.translation: 都市生活的光鲜亮丽对许多农村地区的年轻人来说极具吸引力。

vocabulary.entry: sector /ˈsektə(r)/ n. 行业；领域
vocabulary.example: The technology sector is growing at a rapid pace in this country.
vocabulary.translation: 该国的科技行业正在飞速发展。

vocabulary.entry: destined /ˈdestɪnd/ adj. 注定的；一定会的
vocabulary.example: From an early age, she was destined to become a musician.
vocabulary.translation: 她从小就注定会成为一名音乐家。

vocabulary.entry: shortfall /ˈʃɔːtfɔːl/ n. 缺口；不足

vocabulary.translation: 该国建筑行业正面临技术工人短缺的问题。

vocabulary.entry: catering /ˈkeɪtərɪŋ/ n. 餐饮服务；餐饮业
vocabulary.example: The catering business has expanded significantly since the end of the restrictions.
vocabulary.translation: 限制措施结束后，餐饮业规模大幅扩张。

vocabulary.entry: retail /ˈriːteɪl/ n. 零售业
vocabulary.example: Online retail has changed the way people shop in recent years.
vocabulary.translation: 近年来，线上零售业改变了人们的购物方式。

vocabulary.entry: reality gap /riˈæləti ɡæp/ 现实差距

vocabulary.translation: 毕业生的期望与就业市场的实际情况之间存在巨大的现实差距。

vocabulary.entry: occupation /ˌɒkjuˈpeɪʃn/ n. 职业；工作
vocabulary.example: Please indicate your current occupation on the application form.
vocabulary.translation: 请在申请表上填写你目前的职业。

vocabulary.entry: unlock /ʌnˈlɒk/ v. 发掘；开启；解锁
vocabulary.example: The right training can help unlock a student's hidden talents.
vocabulary.translation: 合适的培训能帮助发掘学生潜在的天赋。

vocabulary.entry: job satisfaction /dʒɒb ˌsætɪsˈfækʃn/ 职业成就感；工作满意度
vocabulary.example: Job satisfaction is often more important than salary for many employees.
vocabulary.translation: 对许多员工来说，职业成就感往往比薪水更重要。

vocabulary.entry: available /əˈveɪləbl/ adj. 可获得的；可找到的
vocabulary.example: There are no tickets available for the concert next weekend.
vocabulary.translation: 下周末音乐会的票已经售罄了。

vocabulary.entry: keen /kiːn/ adj. 热衷的；渴望的
vocabulary.example: She is keen to pursue a career in environmental protection.
vocabulary.translation: 她渴望投身环保行业。

vocabulary.entry: meantime /ˈmiːntaɪm/ n. 与此同时；在此期间
vocabulary.example: The new building is under construction. In the meantime, we will use the old one.
vocabulary.translation: 新大楼正在修建中，在此期间我们会使用旧楼。

vocabulary.entry: aspiration /ˌæspəˈreɪʃn/ n. 抱负；志向
vocabulary.example: Her main aspiration is to start her own business one day.
vocabulary.translation: 她的最大志向是有朝一日创办自己的公司。

vocabulary.entry: veterinarian (vet) /ˌvetərɪˈneəriən/ n. 兽医
vocabulary.example: The vet gave the injured dog a thorough examination and prescribed some medicine.
vocabulary.translation: 兽医给受伤的狗狗做了全面检查，并开了一些药。

vocabulary.entry: sales assistant /seɪlz əˈsɪstənt/ n. 销售助理

vocabulary.translation: 销售助理帮我找到了一双合适的鞋子。

vocabulary.entry: carer /ˈkeərə(r)/ n. 护工；照料者

vocabulary.entry: sales and marketing /seɪlz ənd ˈmɑːkɪtɪŋ/ 销售与市场营销

vocabulary.entry: realistic /ˌriːəˈlɪstɪk/ adj. 现实的；实际的
vocabulary.example: It is important to set realistic goals that you can actually achieve.
vocabulary.translation: 设定切实可行的目标非常重要。

vocabulary.entry: secondary school /ˈsekəndri skuːl/ 中学
vocabulary.example: He attended a local secondary school before going to university.
vocabulary.translation: 他上大学前就读于当地的一所中学。

vocabulary.entry: channel /ˈtʃænl/ v. 引导；把……用于
vocabulary.example: The program aims to channel young people's energy into positive activities.
vocabulary.translation: 该项目旨在将年轻人的精力引导到积极的活动中去。

sentences.chinese: 你小时候想成为什么样的人？

sentences.chinese: 医生、工程师——抑或是足球运动员、演员？

sentences.english: But how realistic was that?

sentences.chinese: 慈善机构“教育与雇主”开展的研究显示，英国17至18岁的青少年中，希望从事艺术、文化、娱乐和体育行业的人数，是这些领域现有岗位数量的五倍之多。

sentences.english: The glamour and excitement of working in these employment sectors is obviously a draw.
sentences.chinese: 这些行业自带的光鲜亮丽与激情活力，显然极具吸引力。

sentences.english: But those looking for these types of job will be ‘destined for disappointment’. That’s what the report, Disconnected: Career aspirations and jobs in the UK, says.
sentences.chinese: 但这份名为《脱节：英国青少年的职业理想与现实岗位》的报告指出，那些一心想进入这些领域的人“注定会失望”。

sentences.english: Writing about this for the BBC, Katherine Sellgren points out that while young people are keen to work in art, entertainment, culture and sport, the economy is unlikely to need them all.
sentences.chinese: 凯瑟琳·塞尔格伦在为英国广播公司撰写的相关报道中指出，尽管年轻人热衷于投身艺术、娱乐、文化和体育行业，但行业并不需要这么多人。

sentences.english: In the meantime, there is a shortfall of young people wanting to work in careers such as catering and retail.
sentences.chinese: 与此同时，愿意从事餐饮、零售等行业的年轻人却存在缺口。

sentences.english: Previous research about the career aspirations of young people by the Office for National Statistics also found a ‘reality gap’ between their dreams and the sometimes disappointing truth by the time they reached their early to late-20s.

sentences.english: Apart from those who aimed to go into teaching, fewer than one in 50 were in the jobs they had wanted – such as a doctor, vet, firefighter or actor.
sentences.chinese: 除了那些立志从教的人之外，只有不到五十分之一的人从事了自己儿时向往的职业——比如医生、兽医、消防员或演员。

sentences.english: Most were working as sales assistants, carers or in sales and marketing.

sentences.english: While it’s good to have aspirations, the aims of young people need to be realistic.
sentences.chinese: 心怀理想固然是好事，但年轻人的目标需要贴合现实。

sentences.english: This latest report suggests that children need to be made more aware of a wider variety of occupations at a younger age.
sentences.chinese: 这份最新报告建议，应该让孩子们在更小的年纪就接触到更多元的职业类型。

sentences.english: It also calls for improved careers advice in secondary schools.
sentences.chinese: 报告还呼吁优化中学阶段的职业规划指导。

sentences.english: A spokeswoman for the Department for Work and Pensions told the BBC that “early careers advice can help young people set out on the right path to the job that channels their interests and unlocks their potential.”
sentences.chinese: 英国就业与养老金部的一位发言人告诉英国广播公司：“尽早提供职业规划建议，能帮助年轻人踏上正确的职业道路，找到能发挥自身兴趣、挖掘自身潜力的工作。”

title: What can you do with used coffee
paragraphs: It's the most popular drink worldwide. According to the British Coffee Association, approximately two billion cups of coffee are consumed every day. But after the beans have been picked, roasted and brewed, the grounds are often disposed of as waste. With the environment and resource consumption such hot topics at the moment, wouldn't it be great if we could reuse this waste to make something useful? Well, you can.

The company OCHIS manufactures sunglasses. Max Havrylenko, founder of the company, was searching for an alternative substance to plastic. He wanted to 'solve the problem of plastic use and overconsumption', he told the BBC. OCHIS fuses the grounds with vegetable oils, forming a bond. These are pressed into plates which are durable and flexible. These are then cut into the arms and frames of the glasses. "Don't worry," he says, "They won't dissolve in the rain."

Rosalie McMillan, a London jeweller, uses recycled coffee grounds along with gold and silver to make handcrafted jewellery. She mixes the coffee with oils and subjects it to heat and pressure to create a compound she calls 'Çurface'. Her website claims it has a 'beautiful surface quality and texture' with similar properties to hardwood.

What about a coffee cup made from them? Kaffeeform is a German-based company that transforms used grounds and renewable plant-based raw materials into a durable composite. This is shaped into a variety of containers and polished and finished, ready to be sold. So, you can drink your coffee from a cup made of coffee.

And it doesn't stop there. Even without a factory, you can make use of coffee grounds. They make excellent fertiliser. You can exfoliate with them, or mix them with water to make a sepia-toned paint. And the list goes on. So next time you finish your morning cup, save the grounds.

vocabulary.entry: grounds /ɡraʊndz/ n. （咖啡或茶冲泡后留下的）残渣
vocabulary.example: She emptied the coffee grounds into the garden to use as fertiliser.
vocabulary.translation: 她把咖啡渣倒进花园，用作肥料。

vocabulary.entry: resource consumption /rɪˈsɔːs kənˈsʌmpʃn/ 资源消耗
vocabulary.example: The government has launched a campaign to reduce resource consumption in households.
vocabulary.translation: 政府发起了一项旨在降低家庭资源消耗的运动。

vocabulary.entry: reuse /ˌriːˈjuːz/ v. 再次使用；重复利用
vocabulary.example: We can reuse glass bottles instead of throwing them away.
vocabulary.translation: 我们可以重复使用玻璃瓶，而不是把它们扔掉。

vocabulary.entry: manufacture /ˌmænjuˈfæktʃə(r)/ v. （大规模）生产；制造
vocabulary.example: The factory manufactures high-quality furniture for export.
vocabulary.translation: 这家工厂生产优质家具用于出口。

vocabulary.entry: alternative /ɔːlˈtɜːnətɪv/ adj. 可供替代的；非传统的
vocabulary.example: We need to find an alternative fuel to replace petrol.
vocabulary.translation: 我们需要找到一种替代燃料来取代汽油。

vocabulary.entry: fuse /fjuːz/ v. 使（不同物质）融合；熔合
vocabulary.example: The artist fused different metals to create a unique sculpture.
vocabulary.translation: 这位艺术家将不同金属融合，打造出一件独特的雕塑。

vocabulary.entry: durable /ˈdjʊərəbl/ adj. 耐用的；持久耐用的
vocabulary.example: This jacket is made of a durable fabric that resists water.
vocabulary.translation: 这件夹克由防水的耐用面料制成。

vocabulary.entry: flexible /ˈfleksəbl/ adj. 柔韧的；易弯曲且不易折断的
vocabulary.example: The flexible material can be bent into any shape.
vocabulary.translation: 这种柔韧的材料可以弯成任意形状。

vocabulary.entry: dissolve /dɪˈzɒlv/ v. 溶解；溶于（液体）
vocabulary.example: This special plastic won’t dissolve in rain or moisture.
vocabulary.translation: 这种特殊塑料不会在雨水或湿气中溶解。

vocabulary.entry: handcrafted /ˌhændˈkrɑːftɪd/ adj. 手工制作的；手工艺品的
vocabulary.example: The shop sells handcrafted pottery made by local artists.
vocabulary.translation: 这家店售卖当地艺术家制作的手工陶器。

vocabulary.entry: compound /ˈkɒmpaʊnd/ n. （化学或工艺中的）复合物；合成物
vocabulary.example: The new compound has both strength and flexibility.
vocabulary.translation: 这种新型复合物兼具强度与柔韧性。

vocabulary.entry: texture /ˈtekstʃə(r)/ n. （材料、物体的）质地；纹理
vocabulary.example: The fabric has a rough texture that feels pleasant to touch.
vocabulary.translation: 这种面料质地粗糙，摸起来很舒服。

title: Houseplants Good or bad
paragraphs: There’s no place like home. It’s the place where we’re surrounded by our possessions and creature comforts. We purchase things to give our homes a personal touch and create a certain ambience. And one thing we’re buying more of is houseplants. But are these ‘living’ additions to our homes good for us and the environment?

Houseplants, also known as pot plants, have Instagram-friendly appeal; add a natural touch and they have the ability to brighten up a room on a budget. The Royal Horticultural Society found that nearly 72% of adults in the UK had a houseplant in their home, with this figure rising to 80% of 16-24 year olds. A fifth of owners also said they use plants in the home to boost their health and well-being. And average sales last year were up on the previous year.

It seems millennials are driving the growth in the sales of houseplants. According to research by The Economist, more young people are living in flats without a garden. 24 year-old Daisy Hale told the BBC "being able to care for something but not having too much commitment - I guess that's a classic millennial line - is ideal for my lifestyle."

From hanging baskets, to cacti and succulent ferns, the choice of vegetation is endless. They are easy to care for, and there have been unproven claims that they improve the air quality in our home. But whatever their benefits, there are now concerns that they are bad for the environment. Alice Vincent, a journalist and author, told the BBC "this could rack up ‘plant miles’".

But botanist and BBC presenter James Wong argues that home delivery has less of an environmental impact than multiple trips to the garden centre in a car. Although he’s not too concerned about the environmental impact, others are worried about the plastic pots they are in and the type of peat that some of them are grown in. However, a sustainable approach to buying them may be the best way forward if we want to introduce some natural greenery into our homes.

title: The pros and cons of flatsharing
paragraphs: Grimy coffee cups, dirty clothes all over the floor and uninvited guests – and they're not even yours! These are the joys of flatsharing. So why do we do it? Well, for many, buying a house or flat is just too expensive. In fact, according to the Guardian, the total amount of rent paid by tenants in Britain in 2017 rose to more than £50 billion – more than double the level of ten years prior. And for those who do, many choose to share the place with strangers to save money. You rent a room and share the kitchen, living room and bathroom, for example. But apart from the financial saving, what are the pros and cons of flatsharing?

The pros? Well, living with others means that you can pool your resources. You may not even need to ask; just leave an IOU. Then there's the fact that you gain access to their social networks. Living with people means meeting their friends, who may then become your friends. And don't forget the networking opportunity. Lastly, there's the emotional support. Due to the nature of communal living, you're not just dealing with your own life events, but other people's too. Most likely, there'll always be a shoulder to cry on when you need one. But don't forget to reciprocate when they need it.

Now the cons. There's limited storage space, for a start. In most cases, the kitchen, for example, will be divvied up into designated shelves and areas. Worse, many people may not respect these boundaries. You might well come home to find someone's pilfered your milk or shower gel, and no one owns up to it. Furthermore, despite the rota showing that cleaning is everyone's responsibility, some people don't like to pull their weight. And then there are the unexpected guests. If a flatmate forgets to keep you in the loop about a party they're throwing and all you want is a quiet night, it can be challenging.

Whether the pros outweigh the cons is something everyone must decide for themselves. Some people prefer their own space, while others thrive in a social environment. Regardless, for many who lack the means to buy their own property, a flatshare is, and will continue to be, a necessity.

vocabulary.entry: grimy /ˈɡraɪmi/ adj. 沾满污垢的；肮脏的

vocabulary.example: He left me an IOU for the money he borrowed.
vocabulary.translation: 他借了我的钱，给我留了一张欠条。

vocabulary.entry: social networks /ˈsəʊʃl ˈnetwɜːks/ 社交圈；社交网络
vocabulary.example: She expanded her social networks by attending industry events.
vocabulary.translation: 她通过参加行业活动拓展了自己的社交圈。

vocabulary.entry: networking opportunity /ˈnetwɜːkɪŋ ˌɒpəˈtjuːnəti/ 拓展人脉的机会
vocabulary.example: The conference is a great networking opportunity for young professionals.
vocabulary.translation: 这场会议对年轻职场人士来说是个拓展人脉的好机会。

vocabulary.entry: emotional support /ɪˈməʊʃənl səˈpɔːt/ 情感支持
vocabulary.example: Her family provided her with emotional support during her illness.
vocabulary.translation: 她生病期间，家人给了她情感上的支持。

vocabulary.entry: communal living /kəˈmjuːnl ˈlɪvɪŋ/ 集体生活
vocabulary.example: Communal living requires everyone to respect the rules of the house.
vocabulary.translation: 集体生活需要每个人都遵守家规。

vocabulary.entry: a shoulder to cry on /ə ˈʃəʊldə(r) tu kraɪ ɒn/ 可以倾诉的对象；能借予慰藉的人
vocabulary.example: When her dog died, her best friend was a shoulder to cry on.
vocabulary.translation: 她的狗去世时，最好的朋友成了她可以倾诉的对象。

vocabulary.entry: reciprocate /rɪˈsɪprəkeɪt/ v. 回报；投桃报李
vocabulary.example: If someone helps you, it's polite to reciprocate.
vocabulary.translation: 如果有人帮了你，礼貌的做法是予以回报。

vocabulary.entry: storage space /ˈstɔːrɪdʒ speɪs/ 储物空间
vocabulary.example: This house has plenty of storage space for all our belongings.
vocabulary.translation: 这栋房子有足够的储物空间放我们所有的东西。

vocabulary.entry: divvy up /ˈdɪvi ʌp/ 分配；分摊
vocabulary.example: We need to divvy up the work between the team members.
vocabulary.translation: 我们需要把工作分配给团队成员。

vocabulary.entry: designated /ˈdezɪɡneɪtɪd/ adj. 指定的；专用的
vocabulary.example: This is a designated smoking area.
vocabulary.translation: 这里是指定吸烟区。

vocabulary.entry: pilfer /ˈpɪlfə(r)/ v. 小偷小摸；偷偷拿走
vocabulary.example: Someone has been pilfering stationery from the office.
vocabulary.translation: 有人一直在从办公室偷文具。

vocabulary.entry: own up to /əʊn ʌp tuː/ 承认（过错）
vocabulary.example: No one owned up to breaking the window.
vocabulary.translation: 没人承认打碎了窗户。

vocabulary.entry: rota /ˈrəʊtə/ n. 值班表；轮值表
vocabulary.example: Can you check the cleaning rota to see whose turn it is today?
vocabulary.translation: 你能看一下清洁值班表，看看今天轮到谁了吗？

vocabulary.entry: pull their weight /pʊl ðeə(r) weɪt/ 尽责；尽本分
vocabulary.example: Some members of the team don't pull their weight.
vocabulary.translation: 团队里有些成员不尽责。

vocabulary.entry: keep you in the loop /kiːp juː ɪn ðə luːp/ 让你知情；让你了解情况
vocabulary.example: Please keep me in the loop about any changes to the plan.
vocabulary.translation: 计划有任何变动，请务必通知我。

vocabulary.entry: property /ˈprɒpəti/ n. 房产；财产
vocabulary.example: He invested all his money in property.
vocabulary.translation: 他把所有的钱都投资到了房产上。

sentences.english: Grimy coffee cups, dirty clothes all over the floor and uninvited guests – and they're not even yours!
sentences.chinese: 沾满污垢的咖啡杯、散落一地的脏衣服、不请自来的访客——这些东西甚至都不是你的！

sentences.english: These are the joys of flatsharing.
sentences.chinese: 这就是合租的“乐趣”所在。

sentences.english: So why do we do it?
sentences.chinese: 那么我们为什么还要选择合租呢？

sentences.english: Well, for many, buying a house or flat is just too expensive.
sentences.chinese: 对很多人来说，买房或买公寓实在太贵了。

sentences.english: In fact, according to the Guardian, the total amount of rent paid by tenants in Britain in 2017 rose to more than £50 billion – more than double the level of ten years prior.
sentences.chinese: 事实上，据《卫报》报道，2017年英国租客支付的房租总额高达500多亿英镑，是十年前的两倍多。

sentences.english: And for those who do, many choose to share the place with strangers to save money.
sentences.chinese: 就算是租房，很多人也会选择和陌生人合租来省钱。

sentences.english: You rent a room and share the kitchen, living room and bathroom, for example.
sentences.chinese: 比如你租下一间卧室，和别人共用厨房、客厅和浴室。

sentences.english: But apart from the financial saving, what are the pros and cons of flatsharing?
sentences.chinese: 但除了省钱，合租还有哪些利弊呢？

sentences.english: The pros?
sentences.chinese: 好处有哪些呢？

sentences.english: Well, living with others means that you can pool your resources.
sentences.chinese: 和别人一起住意味着你们可以共享资源。

sentences.english: You may not even need to ask; just leave an IOU.
sentences.chinese: 你甚至都不用开口求助，留下一张欠条就行。

sentences.english: Then there's the fact that you gain access to their social networks.
sentences.chinese: 此外，你还能接触到室友的社交圈。

sentences.english: Living with people means meeting their friends, who may then become your friends.
sentences.chinese: 和别人同住就意味着会认识他们的朋友，而这些人说不定也会成为你的朋友。

sentences.english: And don't forget the networking opportunity.
sentences.chinese: 还有一点不容忽视，那就是拓展人脉的机会。

sentences.english: Lastly, there's the emotional support.
sentences.chinese: 最后，合租还能带来情感上的支持。

sentences.english: Due to the nature of communal living, you're not just dealing with your own life events, but other people's too.
sentences.chinese: 基于集体生活的属性，你要面对的不只是自己的生活琐事，也会参与到别人的生活中。

sentences.english: Most likely, there'll always be a shoulder to cry on when you need one.
sentences.chinese: 当你需要倾诉时，很可能总会有人愿意借你一个肩膀哭泣。

sentences.english: But don't forget to reciprocate when they need it.
sentences.chinese: 但别忘了，当他们需要帮助时，你也要投桃报李。

sentences.english: Now the cons.
sentences.chinese: 再来说说弊端。

sentences.english: There's limited storage space, for a start.
sentences.chinese: 首先，储物空间会很有限。

sentences.english: In most cases, the kitchen, for example, will be divvied up into designated shelves and areas.
sentences.chinese: 比如大多数情况下，厨房里的架子和区域都会被划分好，分配给每个人专用。

sentences.english: Worse, many people may not respect these boundaries.
sentences.chinese: 更糟的是，很多人可能不会遵守这些界限。

sentences.english: You might well come home to find someone's pilfered your milk or shower gel, and no one owns up to it.
sentences.chinese: 你很可能下班回家后发现，自己的牛奶或沐浴露被人偷偷享用了，却没人承认。

sentences.english: Furthermore, despite the rota showing that cleaning is everyone's responsibility, some people don't like to pull their weight.
sentences.chinese: 此外，即便清洁排班表上写着打扫卫生是每个人的责任，有些人就是不愿尽责出力。

sentences.english: And then there are the unexpected guests.
sentences.chinese: 还有那些不请自来的访客也很让人头疼。

sentences.english: If a flatmate forgets to keep you in the loop about a party they're throwing and all you want is a quiet night, it can be challenging.
sentences.chinese: 如果室友要办派对却忘了告诉你，而你只想安安静静地度过一晚，那场面就会很尴尬。

sentences.english: Whether the pros outweigh the cons is something everyone must decide for themselves.
sentences.chinese: 合租到底是利大于弊还是弊大于利，每个人都得自己做决定。

sentences.english: Some people prefer their own space, while others thrive in a social environment.
sentences.chinese: 有些人更喜欢独处的空间，而有些人则在社交环境中如鱼得水。

sentences.english: Regardless, for many who lack the means to buy their own property, a flatshare is, and will continue to be, a necessity.
sentences.chinese: 但无论如何，对于许多没有能力购置房产的人来说，合租现在是、未来也依然会是一种刚需。

title: A better life
paragraphs: How are you feeling today? Often when we ask people that question, they reply ‘not bad’, or ‘could be worse’. But what would make us feel ‘perfect’? Maybe we could live better by being healthier, less stressed, more motivated – but how?

Of course there are many remedies for improving our mental health, but sometimes there are small and simple solutions to help improve our wellbeing. It’s something the BBC TV programme Easy Ways to Live Well has been looking at. It suggested several ‘health hacks’ which the programme’s presenters tried and gave their ‘seal of approval’. And maybe they could help us too.

Firstly, to tackle putting on weight and to cut the calories, the programme found sniffing peppermint stops our craving for a snack. Presenter, chef and writer Hugh Fearnley-Whittingstall says “a scientific theory called ‘mutual competition’ shows that a strong smell can distract our brain from the food we’re thinking about.”

If your addiction to your smartphone is getting you down, it’s suggested that turning your phone screen grey helps you reduce screen time because a black and white screen becomes less attractive to look at. With recent studies showing our phones can make us 26% less productive and increase our stress, it seems like a no-brainer to try this ‘dim’ idea.

Fancy a swim in ice-cold water? Well, the BBC programme found a daily dip in freezing water gets you used to the stress of doing it and therefore prepares you for other life stresses. And another way to ‘chill out’ is to leave your smartphone at home, immerse yourself in a forest, and breathe in the fresh air. Forest bathing is the perfect tonic for the stresses of urban life.

Other life-improving ideas included things such as singing to reduce pain and fidgeting more to get away from our sedentary lives. But whatever therapy we choose to adopt, it seems any change to our lifestyle can help improve our body and mind.

vocabulary.translation: 均衡饮食和规律运动对身心健康至关重要。

vocabulary.entry: peppermint /ˈpepəmɪnt/ n. 薄荷

vocabulary.entry: craving /ˈkreɪvɪŋ/ n. 渴望；渴求

vocabulary.translation: 她累的时候就特别想吃巧克力。

vocabulary.entry: distract /dɪˈstrækt/ v. 分散注意力；使分心

vocabulary.translation: 选择这家经济实惠的酒店是个明智的决定。

title: The popularity of kosher food
titleChinese: 引领饮食潮流的犹太洁食
paragraphs: Have you ever eaten kosher food? That's food which conforms to the Jewish dietary regulations of kashrut. These regulations forbid consuming pork or shellfish of any kind, for example. Meat from other animals, such as cows and lamb, are okay provided restrictions are met. But they must be slaughtered according to set guidelines. All kosher rulings are overseen by trained rabbis from a kosher certification agency. They inspect, uphold and grant rights to label a food kosher. Ordinarily, kosher food is associated with the Jewish faith, but it's becoming very popular among non-Jews too.

According to the Jewish telegraphic agency, as of 2018 there were approximately 7.5 million Jews in the United States. But, according to a study by the Quartz business news website, 41% of all packaged foodstuffs there are certified kosher. In fact, the global kosher food market is predicted to rise to $60 billion in annual sales by 2025 - according to PR Newswire, a press release distribution network.

Why might this be? One reason is the possible perception that kosher food is cleaner or healthier. Another is the guarantee that certain allergens, such as shellfish, will definitely not be permitted. And its protocols mean anyone seeking to avoid certain ingredients like gelatine, can do so.

“It appeals to a more health-conscious consumer,” says Menachem Lubinsky, CEO of Lubicom. They're the organiser of "Kosherfest", a two-day event that advertises itself as 'the world's largest and most attended kosher-certified products trade show'. In 2019, at its 31st event in New Jersey, attendance was up from the previous year by 800, and 300 new products were on display. In addition, non-Jewish-owned companies from places such as Pakistan, South Korea and Italy were in attendance.

So keep your eyes peeled for an authorised kosher trademark the next time you're food shopping. Based on their popularity to date, it might not be long before we're all eating a little something kosher.

vocabulary.entry: kosher /ˈkəʊʃə(r)/ adj. 符合犹太教饮食规定的；洁食的
vocabulary.example: We bought some kosher sausages for the party.
vocabulary.translation: 我们为派对买了一些洁食香肠。

vocabulary.entry: dietary regulations /ˈdaɪətəri ˌreɡjuˈleɪʃnz/ 饮食规定；膳食条例
vocabulary.example: The school has strict dietary regulations for students with allergies.
vocabulary.translation: 该校针对过敏学生制定了严格的饮食规定。

vocabulary.entry: kashrut /ˈkæʃruːt/ n. 犹太教饮食教规
vocabulary.example: Kashrut specifies which foods Jewish people can eat.
vocabulary.translation: 犹太教饮食教规明确规定了犹太人可以食用的食物种类。

vocabulary.entry: shellfish /ˈʃelfɪʃ/ n. 贝类海鲜（如虾、蟹、牡蛎等）
vocabulary.example: She is allergic to shellfish and can't eat any shrimp or crabs.
vocabulary.translation: 她对贝类海鲜过敏，一点虾和蟹都不能吃。

title: Solving the problem of e-waste
titleChinese: 电子垃圾处理的新方法
paragraphs: One of the problems damaging our planet is the number of things we throw away. Rubbish of all kinds is piling up in landfill and polluting our rivers and oceans. A more recent addition to the list of things we chuck away is e-waste – electronic items that are broken and not recycled. Now solutions are being found to give this stuff a new life.

Many millions of tonnes of televisions, phones, and other electronic equipment are discarded each year, partly because it’s cheaper to replace them than fix them, but also because we lack the skills to repair them. A UN report claims the 50 million tonnes of e-waste generated every year will more than double to 110 million tonnes by 2050, making it the fastest growing waste stream in the world.

However, there’s a growing trend for repair events and clubs which could be part of a solution to the growing amount of electrical and electronic junk. The BBC visited a Restart Project in London, which is one of many found around the world. One of its volunteers, Francesco Calo, said that "this project allows you to reduce waste, extend the life of objects, and it helps people who cannot afford to get rid of items that have developed a fault."

As many electrical items contain valuable metals, another idea is e-waste mining. An experiment at the University of New South Wales involves extracting these materials from electronic gadgets. It’s thought that doing this could be more profitable than traditional mining. With phones typically containing as many as 60 elements, this could be part of the solution to our appetite for new technology.

These projects make total sense - collections of e-waste for recycling are “stagnating or even decreasing” according to Ruediger Kuehr, of the United Nations University. And in countries where there is no legislation, much of it just gets dumped. However, the European Union, for example, is trying to tackle the problem by insisting manufacturers have to make appliances longer-lasting and will have to supply spare parts for machines for up to 10 years.

title: Could robots replace us at work
titleChinese: 机器人能代替我们工作吗？
paragraphs: If you’re in a job performing tedious tasks, you might think that a robot could do the work instead. But perhaps we underestimate how much technology already helps with the activities that we would otherwise have to do. And as artificial intelligence progresses we might find it replaces us in the workplace altogether.

For now, robotic technology is providing a helping hand for businesses, particularly in manufacturing, assisting humans in performing work more efficiently and sometimes more accurately. For online shopping, for example, robots have become essential in giant warehouses. They sort and move millions of objects of all different shapes and sizes, although humans are still needed to pick and distribute the goods.

The advancement of robotics in the workplace is good for some businesses; the ones who research, develop, build and use them. The British government estimates that by 2035, artificial intelligence could add around £630bn to the UK economy. But there are still tasks that robots can’t yet do, and that’s the challenge for companies such as Automata. Its co-founder, Suryansh Chandra, told the BBC that his technology will eliminate boring, repetitive jobs that humans don't like and aren't very good at, and also create new ones that are likely to replace them.

It seems inevitable that robots will eventually be able to do more and more of the jobs that are currently performed by humans, so should we be worried by the rise of the machines? Some experts fear hundreds of thousands of jobs could disappear as robots replace human workers. A report by the OECD suggests that 14% of jobs are "at high risk of automation" and 32% of jobs could be "radically transformed", with the manufacturing sector at the highest risk.
But as complete automation is some way off, for now we’ll have to work side-by-side with our robot colleagues - and manage to get along with them before they learn to kick us out of the door!

title: Can computer translators beat humans
titleChinese: 机器翻译能打败人工翻译吗？
paragraphs: For me, it was bacon. There I was, standing in the streets of Medellin, Colombia, looking hungrily at a delicious empanada. The sign read 'queso y tocino'. Because I'd got my tongue round some essential Spanish vocabulary, I knew that 'queso' was cheese. But 'tocino'? I typed it into my smartphone translation app. What came back? 'Tocino'. I later learned that means 'bacon' in the local lingo.

Computer-assisted translation is popular. Google Translate, for example, is used by more than 500 million people. But while convenient and easy to use, they are hardly perfect. Now, dropping the odd expression now and again is hardly important on an informal conversational level – as might happen to a tourist on holiday. But in more formal circumstances, such as a medical or legal discussion, the wrong vernacular can be disastrous. So, can a computer translator ever equal a human?

The technology has come a long way. These days, people can wear a 'translation earpiece'. These pick up the foreign terminology and translate it directly to the wearer. Andrew Ochoa, chief executive of US start-up Waverly Labs, a producer of one such earpiece, says they work by 'combining a network of algorithms and speech-recognition technology'. But they have limitations. Firstly, there's a delay while the phrase is translated. How long often depends on the connection strength. Secondly, they aren't able to communicate human sentiment well.

Human conversation is subtler than just the words used. It has tone, attitude, nuance, for example. "If you want to create a relationship… you need a human translator to make it sound natural," Zoey Cooper, brand and content director at Wordbank, a global marketing and translation agency, told the BBC.

So, while many professional translators do use computer-assisted translation tools to help them with the repetitive nature of translation, context is important. It might work well for a survey or instruction manual, but for important human-to-human speech, and for the time being at least, better to use a translator, or your message might get garbled or lost in translation.
